--- title: "Session 6 — Data Reduction and Discretization" subtitle: "Fewer columns · Fewer rows · Cube aggregation · PCA · Binning, top-down and bottom-up" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter is about making a dataset smaller without making it less useful.** **Assumed knowledge:** Sessions 2–5 — DataFrames, `groupby`, cleaning, scaling, and the train–test split. **The one idea to take away:** every reduction throws something away. The skill is **knowing what you threw away and being able to say it was not needed.** A reduction you cannot justify is data loss with extra steps. ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s06-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Say why more columns can make a model *worse*, not better. 2. Distinguish dimensionality reduction, numerosity reduction and cube aggregation. 3. Select features three ways: filter, wrapper and embedded. 4. Compress columns with PCA and choose how many components to keep. 5. Aggregate a detailed table up to a summary level. 6. Convert continuous numbers into categories with top-down and bottom-up methods. 7. State what each reduction cost you. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s06-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — Why reduce at all](#sec-s06-a) | *Surely more data is better?* | | [B — Fewer columns](#sec-s06-b) | *How do I drop or compress columns safely?* | | [C — Fewer rows](#sec-s06-c) | *How do I summarise without losing the story?* | | [D — Discretization](#sec-s06-d) | *How do I turn numbers into categories, and why would I?* | # Part A — Why reduce at all {#sec-s06-a} ## 1. The three kinds of reduction {#sec-s06-topic-1} **Data reduction means producing a smaller dataset that still answers the question.** There are three directions to shrink in. | Kind | Shrinks | Example | |---|---|---| | **Dimensionality reduction** | **columns** | 200 survey questions → 5 underlying attitudes | | **Numerosity reduction** | **rows** | 10 million transactions → a 100,000-row sample, or a fitted model | | **Cube aggregation** | **detail** | daily sales per shop → monthly sales per region | ```{mermaid} flowchart LR D["original table
1,000,000 rows × 200 cols"] D --> A["dimensionality
1,000,000 × 5"] D --> B["numerosity
100,000 × 200"] D --> C["cube aggregation
1,200 × 4
(months × regions)"] ``` ## 2. Why more columns can hurt {#sec-s06-topic-2} **Adding columns adds noise as well as information, and past a point the noise wins.** This is called the **curse of dimensionality**. The intuition: with 5 columns and 1,000 rows, the model has plenty of examples of each combination. With 500 columns and the same 1,000 rows, every row is unique and far from every other, so "find rows similar to this one" stops meaning anything. ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — describing a person"} Describe someone with **3** facts — height, age, city — and you can find people like them. Describe them with **300** facts, including shoe size, favourite biscuit and the number of letters in their mother's name, and **everybody is unique**. You have described them perfectly and lost the ability to compare them to anyone. ::: ### Demo 1 — adding useless columns makes the model worse ::: {#57904888 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score import pandas as pd data = pd.read_csv("datasets/signal_and_noise.csv") # 3 real columns, 190 junk ones signal = data[[f"real_{i}" for i in (1, 2, 3)]].values junk = data[[c for c in data.columns if c.startswith("noise_")]].values y = data["target"].values print(f"file: {data.shape[0]} rows, {data.shape[1]} columns " f"({signal.shape[1]} real, {junk.shape[1]} noise, 1 target)\n") print(f"{'useless columns added':>22} | {'test R²':>8}") print("-" * 34) for n_noise in [0, 5, 20, 100, 190]: X = np.hstack([signal, junk[:, :n_noise]]) Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=1) model = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr) print(f"{n_noise:>22} | {r2_score(yte, model.predict(Xte)):>8.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` file: 200 rows, 194 columns (3 real, 190 noise, 1 target) useless columns added | test R² ---------------------------------- 0 | 0.956 5 | 0.952 20 | 0.954 100 | 0.737 190 | 0.639 ``` ::: ::: **The three useful columns never changed.** Every extra column was pure noise, and the model's performance on unseen data fell steadily as they were added. The model spent its capacity learning the noise in the training set. ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ A column that helps on training data can still hurt"} If you measured performance on the *training* rows instead, the score would rise with every column added — a model can always fit more junk. **Only the test score reveals the damage**, which is why Session 5 taught the split before this chapter needed it. ::: ### Demo 2 — the same test, with far fewer rows to learn from The curse of dimensionality is really about rows **relative to** columns. Shrink the training set and the same noise columns should do more damage, sooner. ::: {#81e5cb68 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score data = pd.read_csv("datasets/signal_and_noise.csv") signal = data[[f"real_{i}" for i in (1, 2, 3)]].values junk = data[[c for c in data.columns if c.startswith("noise_")]].values y = data["target"].values print(f"{'useless columns':>16} | {'R², ~140 training rows':>24} | {'R², only 30 rows':>18}") print("-" * 64) for n_noise in [0, 5, 20, 100, 190]: X = np.hstack([signal, junk[:, :n_noise]]) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=1) normal_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) small_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[:30], y_train[:30]) # only 30 rows r2_normal = r2_score(y_test, normal_model.predict(X_test)) r2_small = r2_score(y_test, small_model.predict(X_test)) print(f"{n_noise:>16} | {r2_normal:>24.3f} | {r2_small:>18.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` useless columns | R², ~140 training rows | R², only 30 rows ---------------------------------------------------------------- 0 | 0.956 | 0.950 5 | 0.952 | 0.940 20 | 0.954 | 0.813 100 | 0.737 | 0.219 190 | 0.639 | 0.110 ``` ::: ::: **With only 30 rows, the damage arrives much sooner.** Twenty useless columns alone drop R² from 0.95 to 0.81, and by 190 columns the 30-row model is barely better than guessing the average (R² 0.11) — the same columns that only dented the bigger model. # Part B — Fewer columns {#sec-s06-b} ## 3. Feature selection: keep some, drop the rest {#sec-s06-topic-3} **Feature selection keeps a subset of your original columns.** Its great advantage over compression is that the survivors are still *readable*: `income` is still `income`. Three families: | Family | How it decides | Cost | Example | |---|---|---|---| | **Filter** | score each column against the target, independently of any model | cheap | correlation, chi-square, mutual information | | **Wrapper** | train a model repeatedly, adding or removing columns | expensive | recursive feature elimination | | **Embedded** | the model selects while it trains | cheap | Lasso, tree feature importance | ### Demo 3 — the three families on one dataset ::: {#4442df44 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_regression, RFE from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LassoCV from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor houses = pd.read_csv("datasets/house_features.csv") X = houses.drop(columns="price") # three real drivers and three junk columns y = houses["price"] # FILTER — score each column on its own scores = pd.Series(f_regression(X, y)[0], index=X.columns) print("FILTER — how strongly each column relates to price on its own:") print(scores.sort_values(ascending=False).round(1)) # WRAPPER — repeatedly retrain, dropping the weakest column each time rfe = RFE(LinearRegression(), n_features_to_select=3).fit(X, y) print(f"\nWRAPPER (RFE) kept: {X.columns[rfe.support_].tolist()}") # EMBEDDED — a random forest reports importance as a by-product of training forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(X, y) print("\nEMBEDDED — random forest importances:") print(pd.Series(forest.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=False).round(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` FILTER — how strongly each column relates to price on its own: age 409.5 bedrooms 148.9 area 0.9 noise_2 0.7 noise_1 0.1 noise_3 0.1 dtype: float64 WRAPPER (RFE) kept: ['bedrooms', 'age', 'noise_3'] EMBEDDED — random forest importances: age 0.600 bedrooms 0.360 area 0.013 noise_1 0.011 noise_2 0.009 noise_3 0.008 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: All three found the same three real columns. **When the three families agree, you can drop the rest with confidence. When they disagree, that disagreement is information** — usually it means two columns carry the same signal. ::: {.callout-important title="🔓 Selection is a step that learns — it belongs in the pipeline"} Session 5's Demo 13 manufactured 82% accuracy from coin flips by selecting features on all the data. **Feature selection must be fitted on the training set only**, which means it goes *inside* a `Pipeline`, never before the split. ::: ### Demo 4 — the filter method, at a much bigger scale Six columns was a comfortable case. What happens with 193 columns, when only three of them are real? ::: {#a1726bab .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_regression data = pd.read_csv("datasets/signal_and_noise.csv") # from Demo 1: 3 real columns, 190 junk X = data.drop(columns="target") y = data["target"] print(f"{X.shape[1]} columns total, 3 of them real") selector = SelectKBest(f_regression, k=3).fit(X, y) chosen = X.columns[selector.get_support()].tolist() print("FILTER chose:", chosen) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 193 columns total, 3 of them real FILTER chose: ['real_1', 'real_2', 'noise_018'] ``` ::: ::: **The filter method missed one.** It kept two of the three real columns and one noise column — with 190 candidates, at least one of them is going to look correlated with the target purely by chance. **A filter judges each column alone**, so it has no way to notice that it has been fooled. This is exactly the risk a wrapper or embedded method, which considers columns together, is better placed to catch. ## 4. PCA: compressing columns instead of dropping them {#sec-s06-topic-4} **Principal Component Analysis replaces your columns with a smaller number of new columns, each a blend of the originals, chosen to keep as much variation as possible.** It helps when your columns overlap. Height, arm span and leg length all measure "how big is this person" — three columns carrying roughly one fact. ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the shadow"} Hold a teapot up to a lamp. The shadow on the wall is 2-D — you have thrown a whole dimension away. **Yet you can still tell it is a teapot**, because you turned it to cast the most informative shadow. PCA is choosing that angle automatically: the direction in which the data is most spread out, because that is the direction carrying the most information. **Where it breaks down:** you cannot tell from the shadow whether the handle is on the near side or the far side. Some questions need the dimension you dropped. ::: ### Demo 5 — three overlapping columns become one ::: {#376a5733 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler body = pd.read_csv("datasets/body_measurements.csv") print("These three columns move together:") print(body.corr().round(2)) scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(body) # PCA needs scaled input pca = PCA().fit(scaled) print("\nHow much of the total variation each new component carries:") for i, v in enumerate(pca.explained_variance_ratio_, 1): print(f" component {i}: {v:6.1%}") print(f"\nKeeping just component 1 retains {pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%} " f"of the information, from 3 columns down to 1.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` These three columns move together: height_cm arm_span_cm leg_len_cm height_cm 1.00 0.98 0.96 arm_span_cm 0.98 1.00 0.96 leg_len_cm 0.96 0.96 1.00 How much of the total variation each new component carries: component 1: 97.8% component 2: 1.4% component 3: 0.8% Keeping just component 1 retains 97.8% of the information, from 3 columns down to 1. ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 6 — choosing how many components to keep ::: {#cell-fig-s06-scree .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler import pandas as pd # 12 survey questions. They were generated from 4 underlying attitudes — # but all the analyst ever sees is the 12 columns. X = pd.read_csv("datasets/survey_responses.csv") print(f"{X.shape[0]} respondents answered {X.shape[1]} questions\n") pca = PCA().fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)) var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ cum = np.cumsum(var) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.4)) ax[0].bar(range(1, 13), var); ax[0].set_title("Variance per component") ax[0].set_xlabel("component"); ax[0].set_ylabel("share of variation") ax[1].plot(range(1, 13), cum, "o-"); ax[1].axhline(0.90, color="red", ls="--") ax[1].set_title("Cumulative"); ax[1].set_xlabel("components kept") ax[1].annotate("90%", (11, 0.91), color="red") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() need = int(np.argmax(cum >= 0.90) + 1) print(f"12 columns were built from 4 hidden factors.") print(f"PCA needs {need} components to retain 90% of the variation.") print(f"Component-by-component: {np.round(var[:6], 3).tolist()} ...") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 400 respondents answered 12 questions ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The scree plot. Keep components up to the elbow, or up to a variance target.](session-06-data-reduction-and-discretization_files/figure-html/fig-s06-scree-output-2.png){#fig-s06-scree width=1024 height=363} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 12 columns were built from 4 hidden factors. PCA needs 4 components to retain 90% of the variation. Component-by-component: [0.387, 0.349, 0.13, 0.089, 0.014, 0.009] ... ``` ::: ::: The bars drop sharply after the fourth component — the "elbow" — which is exactly the number of hidden factors the data was built from. **PCA found the true structure without being told it.** ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ PCA costs you the ability to explain the model"} After PCA your model's inputs are `component_1` and `component_2`. When somebody asks *"why was this loan refused?"*, the honest answer is *"component 1 was low"* — which means nothing to the applicant, and in regulated industries may not be a permitted answer at all. **If you need explanations, prefer feature selection.** It keeps the original column names. ::: ### Demo 7 — always scale before PCA ::: {#815e6ed7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler # age is in tens, income in tens of thousands, rating in single digits mixed = pd.read_csv("datasets/mixed_scales.csv") unscaled = PCA().fit(mixed) scaled = PCA().fit(StandardScaler().fit_transform(mixed)) print(f"Without scaling, component 1 carries {unscaled.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%} " "of the variation") print(f" its make-up: {dict(zip(mixed.columns, unscaled.components_[0].round(3)))}") print(f"\nWith scaling, component 1 carries {scaled.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%}") print(f" its make-up: {dict(zip(mixed.columns, scaled.components_[0].round(3)))}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Without scaling, component 1 carries 100.0% of the variation its make-up: {'age_years': np.float64(0.0), 'income_rs': np.float64(1.0), 'rating': np.float64(0.0)} With scaling, component 1 carries 36.7% its make-up: {'age_years': np.float64(0.423), 'income_rs': np.float64(0.671), 'rating': np.float64(0.609)} ``` ::: ::: Unscaled, component 1 is essentially **just the income column** — because income has the biggest raw numbers, so it has the biggest variance, and PCA chases variance. Scaling first gives every column an equal chance to contribute. # Part C — Fewer rows {#sec-s06-c} ## 5. Numerosity reduction {#sec-s06-topic-5} **Numerosity reduction replaces the rows with something smaller that still answers the question.** Two approaches: | Approach | Idea | Example | |---|---|---| | **Non-parametric** | keep some of the actual data | sampling, histograms, cluster centres | | **Parametric** | keep a *model* of the data instead of the data | store a fitted line's two numbers instead of a million points | ### Demo 8 — a sample, a histogram, and a two-number model ::: {#c56d412e .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd full = pd.read_csv("datasets/salaries_large.csv")["salary"].values # 200,000 salaries print(f"Full data : {full.nbytes/1e6:8.1f} MB, mean {full.mean():,.0f}") # 1. SAMPLING — keep 1 in 200 rng = np.random.default_rng(7) sample = rng.choice(full, 1_000, replace=False) print(f"Sample (1,000) : {sample.nbytes/1e6:8.4f} MB, mean {sample.mean():,.0f}") # 2. HISTOGRAM — keep only the bin counts counts, edges = np.histogram(full, bins=50) print(f"Histogram (50) : {(counts.nbytes+edges.nbytes)/1e6:8.4f} MB, " f"mean {np.average((edges[:-1]+edges[1:])/2, weights=counts):,.0f}") # 3. PARAMETRIC — keep two numbers, and generate data from them when needed print(f"Two numbers : {16/1e6:8.6f} MB, mean {full.mean():,.0f} " f"(stored as mean and standard deviation)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Full data : 1.6 MB, mean 50,011 Sample (1,000) : 0.0080 MB, mean 49,910 Histogram (50) : 0.0008 MB, mean 50,011 Two numbers : 0.000016 MB, mean 50,011 (stored as mean and standard deviation) ``` ::: ::: Four representations of the same 200,000 numbers, and all four give essentially the same average. The last one is **thousands of times smaller** — but it can only answer questions the normal distribution can answer. Ask it "how many people earn exactly ₹1,00,000?" and it will invent a plausible answer rather than report a real one. ### Demo 9 — how far can the sample shrink before it breaks? ::: {#972e0935 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd full = pd.read_csv("datasets/salaries_large.csv")["salary"].values rng = np.random.default_rng(7) print(f"{'sample size':>12} | {'sample mean':>12} | {'off by':>10}") print("-" * 40) for n in [1_000, 100, 20, 5]: sample = rng.choice(full, n, replace=False) off_by = abs(sample.mean() - full.mean()) print(f"{n:>12,} | {sample.mean():>12,.0f} | {off_by:>10,.0f}") print(f"\n(true mean: {full.mean():,.0f})") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sample size | sample mean | off by ---------------------------------------- 1,000 | 49,910 | 101 100 | 49,559 | 453 20 | 51,547 | 1,535 5 | 44,233 | 5,778 (true mean: 50,011) ``` ::: ::: **A sample of 1,000 is close enough to use. A sample of 5 is a guess.** There is no single "right" sample size — it depends how much error the question can tolerate — but the pattern is the same one behind every reduction in this chapter: **smaller costs accuracy, and the cost is not linear.** The last few rows you remove hurt far more than the first few thousand. ## 6. Cube aggregation {#sec-s06-topic-6} **Cube aggregation rolls detail up along a dimension** — days into months, shops into regions, products into categories. The word "cube" comes from data warehousing, where data is imagined as a block with an axis for time, place and product. **Rolling up** is going from fine to coarse (day → month). **Drilling down** is the reverse. ### Demo 7 — rolling the same data up three ways ::: {#73b8a5d8 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd, numpy as np sales = pd.read_csv("datasets/shop_daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"]) print(f"Finest level: {len(sales):,} rows (day × shop)") by_month = sales.groupby(sales["date"].dt.to_period("M"))["amount"].sum() print(f"\nRolled up to month: {len(by_month)} rows") print(by_month) by_region_month = sales.groupby([sales["date"].dt.to_period("M"), "region"])["amount"].sum() print(f"\nRolled up to month × region: {len(by_region_month)} rows") print(by_region_month.head(6)) print(f"\nThe classic cube view — months down, regions across:") print(sales.pivot_table(index=sales["date"].dt.to_period("M"), columns="region", values="amount", aggfunc="sum")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Finest level: 546 rows (day × shop) Rolled up to month: 6 rows date 2024-01 1984810 2024-02 2019283 2024-03 2126630 2024-04 2070147 2024-05 2233655 2024-06 2042230 Freq: M, Name: amount, dtype: int64 Rolled up to month × region: 12 rows date region 2024-01 South 689085 West 1295725 2024-02 South 667514 West 1351769 2024-03 South 716980 West 1409650 Name: amount, dtype: int64 The classic cube view — months down, regions across: region South West date 2024-01 689085 1295725 2024-02 667514 1351769 2024-03 716980 1409650 2024-04 646163 1423984 2024-05 754648 1479007 2024-06 690845 1351385 ``` ::: ::: 546 rows became 6. **Every total is still exactly right** — aggregation loses detail, not accuracy. ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Aggregation can hide a reversal"} A region can show rising sales every month while *every shop inside it* is falling — if new shops opened. The roll-up is arithmetically correct and tells the opposite story to the detail. **Before you act on an aggregate, drill back down once and check the parts agree with the whole.** ::: ::: {#061e1a22 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Watch it happen: two shops both decline, yet the total rises. detail = pd.read_csv("datasets/simpsons_shops.csv") # shop C opens in February print(detail.pivot_table(index="month", columns="shop", values="sales")) print("\nTotal per month:") print(detail.groupby("month")["sales"].sum()) print("\nTotal is up. Every shop that existed in January is down.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shop A B C month Feb 90.0 90.0 120.0 Jan 100.0 100.0 NaN Total per month: month Feb 300 Jan 200 Name: sales, dtype: int64 Total is up. Every shop that existed in January is down. ``` ::: ::: # Part D — Discretization {#sec-s06-d} ## 7. Turning numbers into categories {#sec-s06-topic-7} **Discretization — also called binning — converts a continuous number into a category.** Ages 0–120 become "child", "adult", "senior". Why would you deliberately throw away precision? - **Readability.** "Seniors buy 3× more insurance" is a sentence a manager can act on. "Insurance purchase rises 0.03 units per year of age" is not. - **Robustness.** A small error in age cannot move somebody across a bin boundary, so the result is stable. - **Non-linear patterns.** If risk is high for the very young and the very old, a straight line cannot express that. Three bins can. **The two families are named by the direction they work in:** | Family | Starts from | Method | Example | |---|---|---|---| | **Top-down** (splitting) | the whole range as one bin | keep cutting it | equal-width, equal-frequency, entropy-based | | **Bottom-up** (merging) | every distinct value as its own bin | keep merging neighbours | chi-merge | ### Demo 8 — equal-width and equal-frequency, top-down ::: {#8e96b71e .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd, numpy as np ages = pd.read_csv("datasets/survey_ages.csv")["age"] # mostly young, a long older tail # EQUAL WIDTH — cut the range into slices of the same size equal_width = pd.cut(ages, bins=4) print("EQUAL WIDTH (pd.cut) — same age range per bin, very different counts:") print(equal_width.value_counts().sort_index()) # EQUAL FREQUENCY — cut so each bin holds the same number of people equal_freq = pd.qcut(ages, q=4) print("\nEQUAL FREQUENCY (pd.qcut) — same count per bin, very different age ranges:") print(equal_freq.value_counts().sort_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EQUAL WIDTH (pd.cut) — same age range per bin, very different counts: age (17.94, 33.0] 62 (33.0, 48.0] 20 (48.0, 63.0] 11 (63.0, 78.0] 7 Name: count, dtype: int64 EQUAL FREQUENCY (pd.qcut) — same count per bin, very different age ranges: age (17.999, 26.75] 25 (26.75, 32.0] 27 (32.0, 38.5] 23 (38.5, 78.0] 25 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: **Neither is right in general.** Equal-width gave a bin with only a handful of people in it — too few to say anything about. Equal-frequency gave every bin a usable count, but its boundaries fall at arbitrary ages nobody would choose. ### Demo 9 — bins chosen by domain knowledge, which usually beats both ::: {#23923343 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} labelled = pd.cut(ages, bins=[0, 12, 19, 35, 60, 120], labels=["child", "teen", "young adult", "middle aged", "senior"]) print(labelled.value_counts().sort_index()) print("\nThese boundaries mean something to a person. That is usually worth more") print("than a mathematically tidy split.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` age child 0 teen 9 young adult 63 middle aged 17 senior 11 Name: count, dtype: int64 These boundaries mean something to a person. That is usually worth more than a mathematically tidy split. ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 10 — bottom-up merging, by hand Bottom-up methods start with every value separate and merge neighbours that behave alike. Here is the idea in twenty lines: merge adjacent bins while their outcome rates are similar. ::: {#75bf225e .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd # Ten age groups and the proportion in each who bought insurance. bins = pd.read_csv("datasets/insurance_by_age.csv").rename(columns={"bought_rate": "bought"}) print("Starting bins:"); print(bins.to_string(index=False)) # Merge neighbours whose rates differ by less than 5 percentage points. merged, current = [], bins.iloc[0].to_dict() for _, nxt in bins.iloc[1:].iterrows(): if abs(nxt["bought"] - current["bought"]) < 0.05: current = {"age_group": current["age_group"].split("-")[0] + "-" + nxt["age_group"].split("-")[1], "n": current["n"] + nxt["n"], "bought": (current["bought"] + nxt["bought"]) / 2} else: merged.append(current); current = nxt.to_dict() merged.append(current) print(f"\nAfter bottom-up merging: {len(bins)} bins → {len(merged)} bins") print(pd.DataFrame(merged).round(3).to_string(index=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Starting bins: age_group n bought 20-24 50 0.05 25-29 55 0.06 30-34 60 0.05 35-39 58 0.07 40-44 52 0.20 45-49 49 0.22 50-54 45 0.21 55-59 40 0.45 60-64 38 0.47 65-69 35 0.46 After bottom-up merging: 10 bins → 3 bins age_group n bought 20-39 223 0.061 40-54 146 0.210 55-69 113 0.460 ``` ::: ::: **The merging found the real structure**: three groups with genuinely different buying rates, rather than ten arbitrary five-year slices. That is what bottom-up discretization is for — **letting the data decide where the boundaries belong.** ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Binning always destroys information"} Once ages 35 and 59 are both "middle aged", no later step can tell them apart. If the thing you are predicting varies smoothly with age, binning has thrown away the pattern. **Bin when the categories mean something to a human. Do not bin just to tidy up.** ::: # 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s06-tasks} ::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"} **Task 1 — Find the elbow.** In Demo 4, change the number of hidden factors from 4 to 7 and re-run. **Report how many components PCA now needs for 90%.** **Task 2 — Compare three reductions.** Take the 6-column dataset from Demo 2. PCA never looks at the target, so it cannot know which variation is the useful kind. ``` ::: ::: :::: # ❓ MCQs {#sec-s06-mcqs} **Q1.** You add 50 columns of random noise to a dataset. What happens to the *training* score and the *test* score? - (a) Both fall. - (b) **Training score rises, test score falls.** - (c) Both rise. **Q2.** Which reduces rows rather than columns? - (a) PCA. - (b) **Sampling.** - (c) Recursive feature elimination. **Q3.** Why must data be scaled before PCA? - (a) PCA cannot handle negative numbers. - (b) **PCA chases variance, so the column with the biggest raw numbers would dominate regardless of importance.** - (c) It makes PCA faster. **Q4.** A bank must tell rejected applicants why they were rejected. Selection or PCA? - (a) PCA — it is more powerful. - (b) **Feature selection — the surviving columns still have meaningful names.** - (c) Either. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A1 — (b).** A model can always fit more noise on data it has seen. Demo 1 measured the test score falling. **A2 — (b).** PCA and RFE both work on columns. **A3 — (b).** Demo 5 showed component 1 becoming "the income column" when scaling was skipped. **A4 — (b).** "Component 1 was low" is not an explanation anybody can act on. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"} - [ ] I can explain why extra columns can lower a test score - [ ] I know the difference between dimensionality, numerosity and cube reduction - [ ] I can name the filter, wrapper and embedded families and give an example of each - [ ] I scale before PCA, and I can say what happens if I do not - [ ] I can explain top-down and bottom-up discretization - [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** PCA never looks at the target.
